column2: The aged who see the settled truth call self-control the highest good; for a brahmana especially, self-control is eternal dharma.
For one who is not self-controlled, no rite is rightly accomplished; self-control surpasses giving, sacrifices and study.
Self-control increases energy, and self-control is the supreme purifier; freed from sin and joined with energy, a man gains the great.
Hereafter too, lord of men, he gains the highest happiness; joined with self-control, he attains great dharma.
The self-controlled sleeps happily and wakes happily; he moves happily through the worlds, and his mind is serene.
The man not self-controlled meets constant affliction, and puts forth many other evils born of his own faults.
Among the four stages of life, self-control alone is called the highest vow; I shall tell its marks, of which self-control is the sum.
Forbearance, steadiness, non-violence, equanimity, truth, honesty, mastery of the senses, skill, gentleness, modesty, freedom from restlessness,
freedom from meanness, from violent effort, contentment, pleasant speech, freedom from contentiousness and from envy: self-control is the sum of these.
Honouring the teacher, Kauravya, compassion for beings, freedom from backbiting, avoiding gossip, lies, praise and blame,
desire, anger, greed, arrogance, stiffness, boasting, delusion, envy and contempt: the self-controlled does not indulge these.
Unblamed, free of desire, of small wants and without envy, such a man is like the ocean, never filled.
I am in you, you are in me, and I am in them: through earlier ties and connections, the self-controlled does not practise this.
All the activities of village and forest in the world: he who relies on neither blame nor praise is freed.
One who is friendly, endowed with good character, with good companions, and freed from the various attachments gains a great fruit hereafter.
One of good conduct, with good character, serene of soul, a knower of the self, the wise, gains honour here and reaches a good end.
The good deed done here and practised by the good: that same is the dharma of the sage joined with knowledge, and it does not fail.
Going forth and taking to the forest, joined with knowledge and master of the senses, awaiting the time, so roaming he becomes fit for Brahman.
He from whom beings have no fear, and through whom beings have no fear, released from the body, has no fear from any quarter.
He neither heaps up deeds nor gathers them; equal toward all beings, let him go the way of Maitrayana.
As the course of birds in the sky or of water creatures in water is not seen, so is his, without doubt.
The man who, leaving his house, king, turns to liberation alone, has radiant worlds appointed for him for everlasting years.
Having renounced all actions, renounced austerity according to rule, renounced the various kinds of knowledge, and indeed renounced everything,
not returning to desires, serene of soul, a knower of the self, pure, he gains honour here and reaches heaven.
And the seat of the Grandfather, born of the mass of Brahman, hidden in the cave always, is reached by self-control.
For the awakened one who delights in knowledge and is hostile to no being, there is no fear of return here; whence fear in the next world?
There is only one fault in self-control, and no second is found: that people regard one joined with forbearance as powerless.
But of this fault, greatly wise one, there is a very great merit: in forbearance are vast worlds, easy to gain for the patient.
What need has the self-controlled of the forest, and likewise the one not self-controlled, Bharata? Wherever the self-controlled man dwells, that is the forest, that is the hermitage.
[Vaishampayana said:] Hearing this speech of Bhishma, King Yudhishthira became delighted, as if sated with nectar.
And he asked again Bhishma, best of those who uphold dharma, about austerity, and Bhishma told him everything, bull of the Kurus.

Whatever is hard to obtain, hard to learn, hard to approach, hard to endure, all that can be won by austerity, for austerity is hard to surpass.
mahabharata:12:155.6	The drinker of liquor, the taker of what is not approved, the killer of a foetus, the violator of a teacher's bed: a man is freed from sin by austerity well performed alone.
mahabharata:12:155.7	Austerity has many forms, proceeding by these and those doors; for one who lives in withdrawal, there is no austerity higher than fasting.
mahabharata:12:155.8	Non-violence, truthful speech, giving, and restraint of the senses: from these, great king, there is no austerity higher than fasting.
mahabharata:12:155.9	Nothing is harder than giving, no stage of life is beyond measure; there is nothing higher than the knowers of the three Vedas; renunciation is the supreme austerity.
[Yudhishthira said:] "What is the mark of truth, king, or how is it attained? What comes of attaining truth, and how is it declared?"
[Bhishma said:] "A mixing of the duties of the four classes is not praised; truth is the least changeable among all classes, Bharata.
Truth is always the dharma among the good; truth is eternal dharma; one should bow to truth alone, for truth is the supreme goal.
Truth is dharma and the practice of austerity; truth is eternal Brahman; truth is said to be the supreme sacrifice; everything is founded on truth.
I shall tell you, in due order, the practices and the marks of truth here, in proper sequence.
You should hear how truth is attained; truth is thirteenfold in all the worlds, Bharata.
Truth, equanimity, self-control, without doubt, freedom from envy, forbearance, modesty, endurance, freedom from malice,
renunciation, meditation, nobility, firmness ever steady, and non-violence, king of kings: these are the thirteen forms of truth.
Equanimity toward oneself, toward the unwished, and toward the enemy; having reached the destruction of wish and aversion, and of desire and anger;
self-control, no craving for others' things, steadiness and depth, fearlessness, calming of anger: this is gained by knowledge.
The wise call giving, and restraint in dharma, freedom from envy; one should be free of envy by being ever established in truth.
Of impatience and forbearance, pleasant and unpleasant things here, the good man bears all sides, and the truthful gains the good.
The modest man does good deeply and never boasts; he is ever calm of mind; modesty is gained from dharma.
Endurance bears for the sake of dharma and wealth; this is called patience, but for the support of the world it is gained by steadiness.
Renunciation is the giving up of affection and likewise of objects; it comes to one free of attachment and aversion, not otherwise.
Nobility is the doing, with effort, of good deeds toward beings, without form, and indeed freedom from attachment.
Firmness is not undergoing change in pleasure or pain; the wise man who wishes his own prosperity should always cultivate it.
One should be forbearing in every way, and devoted to truth; freed from joy, fear and anger, the wise man attains firmness.
Non-injury to all beings in deed, mind and speech, favour and giving: this is the eternal dharma of the good.
These thirteen forms, each marked by truth alone, resort to truth here and strengthen it, Bharata.
The end of the virtues of truth cannot be told, Bharata; therefore brahmanas, with the ancestors and gods, praise truth.
There is no dharma higher than truth, no sin higher than falsehood; truth is the foundation of dharma; therefore one should not neglect truth.
From truth come giving, and sacrifices with gifts, vows, the fire-offering, the Vedas, and the other determinations of dharma.
A thousand horse sacrifices and truth were weighed in the scales; and truth alone outweighed a thousand horse sacrifices."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Greed, envy, jealousy, contempt, malice and pity: tell me all this, greatly wise one, as it truly is."
[Bhishma said:] "These thirteen very powerful enemies of living beings are remembered; together, great king, they attend upon men here.
Vigilant, they drive the heedless man, like wolves, and seeing a man other than themselves, they plunder him.
From these sorrow proceeds, from these sin proceeds; a mortal should always know this, bull of the Bharatas.
Their rise, their seat and their decay, best of men: well, I shall relate them; hear it as I tell it.
From greed anger arises, and is stirred by the faults of others; it stays through forbearance, king, and the fortunate turn from it.
From conception desire is born, and grows by being indulged; it ceases by seeing the fault, and by the knowledge of truth in the wise.
The dull-minded see the shastras as contradictory; from that, contentiousness arises, and it ceases through knowledge of truth.
Murderousness arises from anger, greed and habit; and by compassion for all beings, through disgust, it ceases.
From the abandonment of goodness comes malice, and a man does what is harmful; this wanes, dear, by serving the good.
Pride arises in embodied beings from family, knowledge and power; when these are understood, pride perishes at once.
Envy arises from desire and from rivalry, Bharata; in other mortals it perishes by wisdom.
Contempt arises, king, from delusion and from disagreeable, incoherent words of those outside the world; it is stilled by indifference.
Jealousy arises, intense, toward the powerful wrongdoer whom one cannot repay; it ceases through pity.
Pity arises from constantly seeing the wretched; when one knows the firm basis of dharma, that pity is stilled.

These are said to be conquered, and the thirteenth by tranquillity. For these thirteen are all the faults of the sons of Dhritarashtra; you have ever conquered them wholly, and you will conquer them."
[Yudhishthira said:] "As men avoid thorns, a well and fire, so men avoid a man of cruel deeds.
The cruel man is ever lowest, here and hereafter, Bharata; therefore tell me, Kauravya, the determination of dharma about him."
[Bhishma said:] "He who is envious, secretive, known by his deeds, who reviles and is reviled, who binds and is bound,
who proclaims his gifts, uneven, petty, deceitful, crafty, not sharing, proud, clinging and boastful,
suspicious of everyone, harsh, foolish, mean, who always praises his own group and creates discord among the stages of life,
who always delights in harm, makes no distinction between virtue and fault, a great liar, self-regarding, greedy, excessively cruel,
who thinks the virtuous one, of good character, to be bad, and by inference from his own character trusts no one,
who reveals what is secret wherever there is fault in others, and, where faults are equal, harms for the sake of livelihood,
and thinks even the benefactor to be cheated, and though he gives wealth in time grieves for the benefactor,
who eats food, drink, lickables and other good fare while others look on: they know him as cruel.
He who, having given the first portion to brahmanas, eats with his friends gains heaven hereafter, and here gains the endless.
This cruel man has been described to you, best of the Bharatas; he is always to be avoided by one who wishes to prosper."
[Bhishma said:] "These, seen to be good, are brahmanas who live by dharma-alms; to them, from one's own property, giving is to be done, especially learning.
Elsewhere the sacrificial fee, best of the Bharatas, should be given; to others, outside the altar, uncooked food is not ordained.
A king should present all jewels in due measure, and to brahmanas and sacrifices, with food and with fees.
He who has food for three years sufficient for his servants' maintenance, or even more, is fit to drink soma.
If a sacrifice is pierced, with a single limb defective, for the sacrificer, especially a brahmana, while the king is righteous,
the vaishya who has many cattle but omits sacrifices and does not drink soma, from his household the king may take that wealth for the sacrifice.
He may take something from a shudra's house at will, from his goods; for in a shudra's house no one has any possession.
From one with a hundred cows who has not set up the fires, and one with a thousand who does not sacrifice, he may take from both households without hesitation.
For through the kshatriya's childishness a brahmana is afflicted by hunger; knowing his learning and character, he should assign a livelihood, and then protect him as a father his own son.
He should ever offer the Vaishvanari offering at the turn of the year; formerly dharma was without alternative, but now only in the words of dharma.
By all the gods, the Sadhyas, brahmanas and great sages, in fear of death in calamities, a substitute for the mark was made.
He who, able to follow the first course, lives by a substitute, the fruit for the next world is not for that ill-minded man.
No man should instruct brahmanas before a king; the weak man learns from instruction, the strong from the stronger.

Therefore the king should always regard the hard-to-bear energy of the Brahman-speakers; a brahmana is called a god, counsellor, ruler and ordainer; one should say nothing ill of him and not utter a curt word.
The kshatriya crosses his calamity by the strength of his arms, the vaishya by wealth, the shudra, and the twice-born by mantras and oblations.

Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one without mantras, nor a fool, nor an uninitiated person should tend the fire-offering; those who offer fall to hell, and so does the one whose offering it is.
Without giving the Prajapatya horse as the fee for setting up the fires, he is called one who has not set up the fires, say the seers of dharma.
One should do other meritorious acts with faith, master of the senses, but never perform sacrifices whose fees have not been given.
A sacrifice without a fee destroys offspring, cattle and heaven; it cuts off one's senses, fame, glory and life.
Those who live with menstruating women, those who keep no fires, and those whose families are not learned: all these follow the dharma of a shudra.
A brahmana who lives twelve years in a village with water from a well and with a shudra woman as his wife falls to the work of a shudra.
One who keeps an ignoble woman in his bed and one who casts off a twice-born woman, thinking himself a non-brahmana, would sit on grass behind; thus he is purified, king; hear my word on this.
A brahmana who serves a black-coloured woman and commits sin in one night, moving about by standing and sitting, keeping a vow, would remove his sin in three years.
Speech in jest does no harm, nor with women, king, nor at marriage, nor for the sake of a teacher, nor to save one's life: these five untruths are called not sinful.
With faith one may take up auspicious knowledge even from a low source, and one may take gold even from the impure: such is the rule.
A jewel of a woman even from a low family; one may drink nectar even from poison; for it is by dharma that blameless women are jewels.
For the good of cows and brahmanas, and in the mixing of classes, a vaishya may take up a bow, and to protect himself.
Drinking liquor, killing a brahmana, violating a teacher's bed: these are held unatonable, ending in death, such is the rule.
Stealing gold, theft, association with brahmanas, wandering in drink, and approaching the forbidden: these are sins.
By union with the fallen, even a brahmana, by birth, in no long time, great king, becomes like them.
One falls in a year who lives with the fallen, by officiating, teaching and marriage, but not by vehicle, seat or food.
These and others are held to be those for which atonement is prescribed; by the prescribed rule, in time one may become free of fault.
Food should not be offered obliquely in funeral rites for one not fallen; in the first three of these there should be no deliberation.
A righteous man should in accordance with dharma abandon even ministers or teachers; one should not have dealings with those who do not do atonement.
One who does adharma destroys the sin by dharma and austerity; one who calls a man a thief incurs the sin of a thief; one who calls a non-thief a thief incurs double sin.
A maiden who is defiled takes a third of the sin of brahmin-slaying; he who defiled her takes the rest of the sin.
Raising a weapon against a brahmana and touching him becomes heavier; the sinner finds no footing for a hundred years.
But having struck him down he dwells in hell for a thousand years; therefore one should neither raise a weapon nor ever strike him down.
As many grains of dust as take up the blood from a wounded twice-born, for so many years, king, he is turned about in hell.
The killer of a foetus is purified in the midst of battle, struck down by a weapon; he is purified also by offering himself in a kindled fire.
The drinker of liquor, drinking hot Varuni, is freed from sin; his body burnt by it, he is purified after death, and a brahmana gains the worlds; he gains them in no other way.
One who violates a teacher's bed, evil-souled, sinful of mind, is purified by embracing a blazing iron figure and dying.
Or, taking his organ and testicles in his own hands, he should go toward the south-west and fall, and so go straight.
Or he may give up his life for a brahmana's sake and be purified by that; or by performing the horse sacrifice, or the cow sacrifice, or the Agnishtoma rightly, he is purified here and hereafter.
Likewise the killer of a brahmana should be a skull-bearer for twelve years; a celibate student, he should go begging, proclaiming his own deed, as a sage.
Or joined with austerity in this way, the killer of a brahmana may be a dweller in the forest; and one who unknowingly approaches an Atreyi incurs double the guilt of brahmin-slaying.

The drinker of liquor, of restrained diet, a celibate student, practising forbearance, after three years may conquer by the highest Agnishtut; having given a thousand cows and a bull, he gains the good.
Having killed a vaishya, he does two years' penance and gives a hundred cows and a bull; having killed a shudra, one year and ten cows and a bull.
Having killed a dog, a boar, or an ass, he should perform the shudra's vow; likewise for a cat, a chasha bird, a frog, a crow, a bhasa bird or a mouse.
The dharma for killing an animal is said to be like that for a beast, king; I shall now tell other atonements in order.
For another's bed and for theft, one should do penance separately for a year; for the wife of a learned brahmana three years, and for another's wife two.

Eating at the fourth time, he should be a celibate vow-keeper, moving by standing and sitting, three times a day taking water from the risen sun; so too he who is without rinsing and throws away the fires.
He who without cause abandons his father and mother becomes fallen, Kauravya; such is the settled rule in dharma.
She should be given food and clothing in plenty: so the example goes. For an unchaste wife who is confined, especially, whatever vow is prescribed for men with others' wives, let her perform that.
The woman who leaves a better man in bed and goes to a worse one, the king should have her eaten by dogs in a place well enclosed.
The wise king should have the man bound on a heated iron bed; they should put wood on it, and the sinner is burned there.
This is the punishment, great king, for women who transgress against the husband; for the accused for a year, the punishment of the wicked would be double.
Two for him, three years; four for one who serves with him; five years for a bad walker; he should go begging, keeping the vow of a sage.
A younger brother married before his elder, the elder, the woman by whom this occurs, and the one who takes her hand: all these are remembered as fallen.
All of these should perform the vow that the killer of a hero performs: let him perform the Chandrayana for a month, or the Krichchhra, for purification from sin.
The one who married first should give that daughter-in-law to the elder; the younger, with the elder's permission, then gains release from sin, and she and both of them, according to dharma.
Among non-human creatures, except cows, drought does not defile; they know the man as master and eater of animals.
Wearing a garment with its tail raised and taking an earthen vessel, he should go begging at seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
Living there on what he gets, he is purified in twelve days; or he may keep that vow for a year, which is the rule of the unformed.
Among human beings this is the highest atonement; as for giving, he should arrange everything for those attached to words; for non-unbelievers they call one cow equal to one life.
One who has eaten the flesh, urine or excrement of a dog, boar, man, cock or ass is fit for purification.
A soma-drinking brahmana who has smelled the breath of a liquor-drinker should drink water for three days, hot milk for three days, hot ghee for three days, and live on air for three days.
So this eternal atonement has been set forth, especially for the brahmana; it comes about by knowledge of the truth."
[Nakula said:] "Grandsire, it is said that the bow is the best weapon; but in my opinion, knower of dharma, the well-sharpened sword is.
When the bow is shattered, king, and the horses spent, in battle one can protect oneself well with a sword.
A single sword-bearing hero is able to withstand even those who bear bows, maces and spears.
Here I have doubt and great curiosity: what is the best weapon in all battles, king?
How was the sword produced, for whose sake and by whom? Tell me the first teacher of the sword, great-grandsire."
Hearing this speech of the wise son of Madri, joined with all skill, subtle, varied in meaning, and auspicious,
Bhishma then gave a reply with proper voice and syllables, endowed with training and method, to the one who asked, a pupil of Drona.
Bhishma, lying on the bed of arrows, knower of all dharma and master of the science of the bow, spoke to the great-souled Nakula.
Covered in darkness, untouchable, of very deep appearance, soundless and immeasurable, there the Grandfather was born.
That mighty one created the wind, fire and the sun; he created the sky above, and below the earth and the south-west.
The sky with moon and stars, constellations and planets, years, days and nights, seasons, moments and instants.
Then the blessed Grandfather, having set up the body of the world, brought forth sons of the highest radiance.
Marichi the sage, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Vasishtha and Angiras both, and Rudra, the lord and master.
Daksha, the son of Prachetas, brought forth sixty daughters; all of them, Brahmarshis, took up the task of progeny.
From them came all beings, the gods and the hosts of ancestors, the gandharvas and apsarases, and the various rakshasas.
Birds, beasts and fish, frogs, great serpents, and others of various forms and strengths that move in water and on land.
The sprout-born, sweat-born, egg-born and womb-born: so, dear, the whole world, moving and unmoving, came to be.
Having made this creation of beings, the Grandfather of all worlds again joined it with the eternal dharma recited in the Veda.
Established in that dharma were the gods with teachers and priests: the Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sadhyas, Maruts and Ashvins,
Bhrigu, Atri, the Angirases, the Siddhas, Kashyapa rich in austerity, Vasishtha, Gautama, Agastya, Narada and Parvata,
the sages, the Valakhilyas, Prabhasas, Sikatas, Ghritachas, Somavayavyas, Vaikhanasas and Marichipas,
the Akrishtas, Hamsas, the fire-born sages, forest-dwellers and Prishnis stood under Brahma's command.
But the lords of the Danavas, transgressing that command of the Grandfather, did harm to dharma, filled with anger and greed.
Hiranyakashipu, Hiranyaksha, Virochana, Shambara, Viprachitti, Prahlada, Namuchi and Bali,
these and many other Daityas and Danavas with their hosts, transgressing the bridge of dharma, delighted in resolve for adharma.
We are all of equal birth; as the gods are, so are we: taking this as a ground, they competed with the divine sages.

They showed neither love nor pity toward beings, Bharata; transgressing three of the means, they restrained the subjects by the rod; and the best of the asuras, in pride, did not come to agreement with them.
Then the blessed Brahma, attended by the Brahmarshis, was on the back of the Himalaya, in a lovely place with lotus-stars,
a hundred yojanas wide, strewn with gems and pearls; on that best of mountains, son, in a forest of flowering trees, the chief of the gods, Brahma, stood to accomplish the world's aim.
Then at the end of a thousand years the lord made a canopy, prepared by the rule seen in the kalpa and as laid down.
With sages skilled in sacrifice, doing the rite rightly, with the Maruts and with blazing fires, it was spread out.
Adorned with golden sacrificial vessels, resplendent, and surrounded by hosts of gods, the sacrificial circle shone.
It was also adorned with Brahmarshis and with the priests of the assembly; there, I have heard, a most terrible event took place among the sages.
As the moon rises in the clear sky with the stars, so, it is heard, a being rose up, splitting the fire.
It was the colour of a blue lotus, sharp-toothed, thin-bellied, tall, hard to look at, and exceedingly bright.
As it rose, the earth trembled; there the great ocean was stirred with waves and whirlpools.
Meteors fell, great portents; trees shed their branches; all quarters were dim, and an ill-boding wind blew; and beings were repeatedly pained with fear.
Then, seeing that tumultuous marvel arisen, the Grandfather said to the great sages, gods and gandharvas:
I have conceived this being; it is called the sword, mighty, for the protection of the world and the slaying of the enemies of the gods.
Then, casting off that form, it shone as a sword, spotless, sharp-edged, raised like the ender of time.
Then Brahma gave that blazing sword, the restrainer of adharma, to Rudra, blue-throated, bull-bannered.
Then the blessed Rudra, praised by hosts of Brahmarshis, of immeasurable self, taking the sword, took another form.
Four-armed, touching the sky with his head though standing on the earth, with upturned gaze and great phallus, casting flames from his mouth, he changed into many colours, blue, pale and red,
wearing black antelope skin, with a garment of excellent stars of gold, with a third eye on his forehead like the great sun, and two spotless eyes, dark-tawny, shone.
[Bhishma said:] "Here too they cite this ancient tale: how Death was conquered by a householder relying on dharma.
Having come to Mount Meru on the Himalaya's northern side, there was a great golden tree, and there he performed the rite.
It is the custom in our family, dear, for all, bull of the Bharatas, to give the sovereignty to their sons and go to the forest at the end of life, king.
Joined with the Bhojas, Satyaki with the Andhakas, by their numbers the two were slain there, before Krishna's eyes.

You are well-born, king of kings, by your father's conduct and your intelligence, and by this compassion toward all beings, Bharata.
mahabharata:18:3.4	The torments of the sinful were no longer seen there, nor the river Vaitarani, with the false silk-cotton tree.
